title: The Evening Brief: Pentagon purge deepens; courts block Trump orders; Iran war reignites
dek: Thursday brought institutional strain across defense, election systems, and the Iran conflict. The Army lost its civilian leader to a dispute over officer removals; federal judges blocked birthright citizenship and mail ballot rules; and the six-month Iran war renewed with U.S. strikes and Iranian retaliation that killed dozens.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The day's throughline is institutional capacity under pressure: the Pentagon fractured over competing visions of leadership, the election system faces untested infrastructure weeks before voting, and the Iran war shows no circuit breaker as each side responds to strikes with fresh strikes.
bottom_line: Thursday saw three systems strain under competing pressures: the Pentagon fractured by officer removals and competing visions of military leadership; the election system challenged by untested infrastructure, cut funding, and legal blocks to voting rules; and the Iran conflict locked in a strike-retaliation cycle with no exit visible. Federal judges are now the primary brake on election-related executive orders, USPS faces operational questions weeks before ballots ship, and the Pentagon awaits a replacement for Driscoll while Hegseth retains White House support despite the resignation. The coming checkpoints are narrow: Talwani's extension decision on the mail ballot block; whether USPS testing or further whistleblower disclosures reveal operational failures; whether Iran's retaliation crosses Trump's stated escalation threshold; and how quickly a new Army secretary is nominated and confirmed.
body: The Pentagon's internal rupture widened Thursday as fallout from Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation continued. Driscoll had warned the White House repeatedly that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's removal of more than two dozen senior officers was depleting the command pipeline, but his warnings went unheeded. He resigned Monday; a senior defense official told the desk's reporting that Driscoll had served as a buffer between Hegseth and the Army, even if ultimately unable to slow the purge. The Army now lacks Senate-confirmed civilian leadership during active military operations across multiple theaters. The White House statement praised Driscoll as "highly effective" while reaffirming "complete trust" in Hegseth, a formulation that papers over rather than resolves the underlying dispute about institutional priorities.

The Iran conflict entered a new escalation cycle Thursday. The U.S. struck Iranian targets along the southern coast on September 2, killing at least 18 according to Iranian health officials. A missile hit a home in Kuhestak during a wedding celebration, killing four people including two children aged 4 and 16, with at least 68 wounded; U.S. Central Command stated it was targeting a communications tower and that civilians were not targeted. Iran responded hours later with missiles and drones aimed at U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain; Kuwaiti and Jordanian night skies showed interceptors lighting up the dark. The strike campaign marked the resumption of direct combat after a month-long pause in a six-month-old war. Brent crude oil climbed to around $95 per barrel, up more than 30% since fighting resumed. Senior Iran analyst Hamidreza Azizi cautioned that "at some point, one of the sides may see a need to escalate in order to break this cycle," potentially bringing the two sides to full-scale war.

Federal judges blocked two Trump executive orders Thursday, marking the judiciary's continuing role as a check on executive actions affecting elections and citizenship. U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a 35-page ruling blocking Trump's August 6 birthright citizenship order, finding it "almost certainly unconstitutional" under the 14th Amendment. This is the second judicial block of a Trump birthright citizenship order in a year, following a Supreme Court ruling in June against his initial 2025 order. Separately, Judge Indira Talwani is deciding whether to extend a temporary ban on Trump administration mail ballot regulations, with the temporary restraining order expiring next week as states begin mailing ballots. Talwani imposed the temporary block on August 27, citing lack of implementation details from the Postal Service. Both cases are expected to reach the Supreme Court.

Election infrastructure faces operational and legal strain. A USPS whistleblower, represented by Whistleblower Aid, alleged Thursday that the Postal Service is deploying a new election mail system that has not been adequately tested and was rushed to completion in roughly eight weeks instead of one to two years. The system has zero percent failure tolerance at each checkpoint and failed testing, the whistleblower's attorney said. Democratic lawmakers demanded Thursday that the Trump administration restore $39.6 million in congressionally appropriated election security funds, citing cuts that forced a free intelligence service to a paid membership model that "under-resourced communities" cannot afford. With the midterm election nine weeks away, states must determine whether they can absorb the loss of free threat intelligence and whether USPS testing reveals operational gaps.

Other developments: Chevron announced plans to invest over $7 billion to expand Venezuelan oil production to approximately 600,000 barrels per day, more than doubling current output, though experts caution meaningful production gains are years away and require overcoming a decade of infrastructure decay. The DOJ reversed a 28-year-old interpretation of welfare law, requiring all state agencies in jurisdictions receiving TANF funds (exceeding $16.4 billion annually) to report known undocumented immigrants to federal immigration authorities. Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist journalist and activist who led the modern women's movement for seven decades, died at age 92. The House passed the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act 237-169, requiring federally funded universities to certify they do not boycott Israel or restrict students from participating in Israeli programs; the bill heads to the Senate.

On the calendar: Judge Talwani must decide whether to extend the mail ballot rule block before the temporary order expires next week. Robinson's trial in the Charlie Kirk shooting is scheduled for October 23 when a trial date will be set. Whether President Trump views the Iran retaliation as a trigger for the "very hard" strikes he threatened, or signals willingness to negotiate over Strait control, will shape the next 48 to 72 hours.
